newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraqis in Baghdad shrug off news of U.S. attacks.
newsitem.headline: Iraqis in Baghdad shrug off news of U.S. attacks.

text.p: Iraqis in Baghdad on Tuesday shrugged off news of U.S. cruise missile attacks and life went on as normal in the streets of the Iraqi capital.
In Washington, Pentagon officials said a cruise missile attack was launched against Iraqi military targets.
An Iraqi television channel run by President Saddam Hussein's son Uday confirmed U.S. military strikes against targets in Iraq.
Air raid sirens blared in some areas of the capital and anti-aircraft fire was launched from positions in Baghdad, witnesses said, but it was not immediately clear what the fire was aimed at.
Iraqis on the streets said they did not care whether an attack took place or not.

"Whatever America does it will be nothing in comparison to what it did in the war over Kuwait. Their (America's) sabre- rattling finds more of a hearing at home," said a taxi driver on his way to the northern city of Kirkuk.
Shoppers on their way to Jamila, Baghdad's main food market, shrugged off questions on the U.S. missile strike.
"It is a fight between candidates for the U.S. presidency. Whatever they do they will not harm the government. The price, we will pay, we the ordinary people," said a shopper.
Life went on as normal and many Iraqis said they were more concerned about the fate of their country's oil-for-food deal with U.N. than the U.S. raids.
Iraqi officials were not available for comment but Saddam was expected to deliver a speech on the attacks later in the day.
At Nahda, a key bus station in Baghdad, buses and taxis carried passengers to Arbil, the Kurdish stronghold which Iraqi troops and forces of a Kurdish rebel leader captured on Saturday.

At Shorja, Baghdad's commercial hub, several Iraqis lambasted U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali for his decision to delay implementation of Iraq's oil-for-food pact with U.N. signed last May.

Iraqi crude exports, blocked since 1990 crisis over Kuwait, were expected to hit international markets by mid-September. Revenues from the exports, $2 billion over six months, would have been used to ease the suffering of the Iraqi people labouring under U.N. trade sanctions.
Boutros-Ghali's decision, Iraqi traders said, sent prices of essential commodities soaring and the value of Iraqi dinar against the U.S. dollar tumbling, making life harder for millions of Iraqis.
"What has the oil deal to do with politics? It was supposed to be a purely humanitarian offer from the U.N. to help vulnerable Iraqis," said Hamed Salwan, a secondary school teacher.
Many shoppers said they left homes early in the morning to buy essential goods as they feared another surge in prices if the U.N. did not allow the food-for-oil deal to go ahead.
Iraqi officials and media have been trying to allay fears of traders, saying their country's oil deal with U.N. was still standing and discussions to finalise arrangement were continuing in New York.
The government newspaper al-Jumhouriya said Iraq's enemies were spreading rumours that the deal was called off to spur traders to raise prices again.
